changes.text: If you sign in through an identity provider, destructive actions are possible again. The confirmation dialog only ever offered a password field — and an account that signs in through a provider has no local password, while a host declared SSO-only refuses the password routes outright. Every destructive action in the product sat behind a form that could not be filled in, showing a refusal that reads like a mistake.

The dialog now sends you to your provider instead. That route existed the whole time and is careful: it asks the provider to authenticate you afresh, checks on the way back that it really did rather than reusing a session, and that the identity returning is the one signed in. Nothing in the interface offered it. The action you were attempting is not carried across the round trip — run it again when you return, and it will not ask twice.

Third time in two days that a route existed with nothing calling it, and the first that locked an operator out entirely. The new use guard could not see this one either: it checks functions that SEND a request, and a path the browser NAVIGATES to is never sent. It now checks those too.

The phantom node is gone. Adoption read a Talos membership entry — which is named after the node's HOSTNAME, not its UUID — and filed that string as a machine id. The check meant to skip the node it had already recorded compared a hostname against a UUID and was never once true, so your control plane was recorded twice: correctly under its UUID, and again under its hostname at whichever address the membership happened to list first. The second record could never answer, because no certificate is minted for that identity.

Every member is now asked who it is, at each address it reports, in order — the same thing "add a node by address" does with an address you type. It is filed under the UUID it answers with, at the address that answered. That also settles which address gets recorded, which used to be left to the order the cluster happened to report them in.

A member that answers at none of its addresses gets no record and a warning naming it and every address tried. The inventory can now be missing a machine the cluster knows about, and that is the deliberate trade: a record under a key nothing can reach is the phantom above, and it looks adopted.

The same confusion decided the ROLE of a machine added by address: control-plane nodes were filed as workers, and a worker is left out of the etcd reads only control-plane nodes get. Invisible until now, because nothing in the interface could reach that function at all.

When a node does not answer, the journal now says what came back and at which address. It knew all along — the reason is classified and shown per field on the screen — and wrote none of it down, so a real cluster's journal held "the node stopped answering" every interval for hours and nothing else. The address is there because a record can be filed against an address its machine does not answer at, and without it that is indistinguishable from a machine that is switched off.

It says it twice and then stops: once on the first failure, once when the count crosses into down. A node that is down stays down and is asked again every interval, so logging each attempt is the other way to make a journal useless. The raw error goes to the log and the classified sentence to the screen — a gRPC status string in a dashboard cell pushes the actionable part off the edge.

A cluster can be removed again. The route and the API client both had it; nothing on any screen called them, so an imported cluster could not be taken back out. Forgetting removes this installation's record and the secrets derived from it — the cluster itself is untouched, and its machines stay in the inventory without a cluster, because they are machines that still exist.

A node can be added by address. Adoption fills the inventory from the membership the adopted node reports, and records each member under the FIRST address it reports — so a machine reachable at some other address had no way in. The code called this "the always-available second way into the inventory"; it was neither available nor a way.

The guard that exists to stop exactly this was green over both. It reads the whole web interface as one text and asks whether a route's path appears in it — and the API client is part of that text, so a client function nothing calls satisfied it. It now asks the second question separately: does any screen call the client function that issues this route? It found these two on its own.

A cluster you import is now actually watched. Adoption recorded every node it found and asked nobody to look at any of them, so a freshly imported cluster read "not answering" for every machine — including the control plane the import had just authenticated to, because adoption proves it can reach that node before it stores anything. The health column was telling you nothing was there, about a node it had just spoken to.

It took a restart to fix itself, and that is why this looked intermittent. Observers were started for whatever was on disk when the daemon came up, so a cluster imported afterwards stayed invisible until the next restart happened to pick it up. Now a machine gets its observer at the moment it enters the inventory, which is the one place that cannot be forgotten.

The guard for this existed and was aimed one step to the left: it proved that the observer a handler starts outlives the request that started it, after an earlier bug ended them early. Nobody asked whether the import path started one at all. The new test reproduces the operator's own order — daemon running, cluster imported after — and checks the screen rather than the internals.

Three drift guards that compare the web interface against the server no longer accept a renamed leftover. Each matched a name wherever it appeared in the text, so a constant renamed by appending to it — REFUSED_RANGES_LEGACY, or a warning code gaining a suffix — kept them green over exactly the drift they exist to catch. What they still cannot see is now written down and measured, one entry per mechanism, instead of claimed to be nothing.

Built against Talos machinery v1.14, which is what a current cluster actually serves. The previous builds advertised support up to v1.14 while pinning the v1.13.9 library — so this product claimed a Talos whose configuration documents its own library could not read, and the first real cluster it was pointed at failed on exactly that.

A machine configuration is read whole again. v1.16.2 selected the v1alpha1 document and ignored the rest, reasoning that every secret lives in it. That was true of Talos v1.13 and is false of v1.14, where the Kubernetes API-server CA is a document of its own — so that approach would have derived a bundle with the Kubernetes CA missing and refused a control-plane node as a worker. Confidently wrong, which is worse than the error it replaced.

A configuration document this build does not know is now a refusal that names it, says which Talos versions this build was made for, and gives the remedy: upgrade holzkube-manager. Not an Internal error, and not a bundle derived from the parts that happened to be recognised — an unknown document can be the one carrying a secret.

Adoption cannot crash the daemon on a configuration it is handed. machinery v1.14 dereferences five accessors without checking them, so a worker's configuration — which has no API-server CA — panics rather than returning an empty bundle as v1.13 did. The configuration is now asked what kind of node it is before anything is derived, and all five are checked first.

Two new guards keep the pin honest, because the operator updates Talos as soon as a release lands. One runs in the build and refuses a supported range wider than the compiled-in machinery can read; the other asks weekly whether a newer stable machinery exists and fails when one does — scheduled rather than opt-in, because this project already has a drift watcher nobody scheduled.

Adopting a real cluster works. It did not: the first real Talos cluster this product was ever pointed at refused adoption with "Internal error", and the reason was a document adoption does not read. A Talos machine configuration is multi-document YAML — one v1alpha1 document carrying the secrets, and beside it a growing set of typed documents. machinery decodes a typed document only if this build knows its kind, its loader is all-or-nothing, and there is no option to tolerate one. A DiscoveryServiceConfig document, which machinery v1.13.9 does not have at all, therefore failed the whole parse. Every secret adoption needs is in the v1alpha1 document; not one sibling is read.

The machine configuration document is now selected rather than the whole file parsed, using machinery's own discriminator: the document with version v1alpha1 and no kind. Selecting rather than tolerating is what makes this hold for the next document kind Talos ships — tolerating would leave adoption depending on which unknown documents a node happens to carry, and a manager that must know every kind Talos will ever ship is one that breaks on every Talos release.

A node serving no machine configuration document at all is now refused as the wrong node — a 400 that names the remedy — instead of failing to parse and arriving as an Internal error nobody can act on.

An Internal error now names the request, so the line that explains it can be found in the server log. That family strips its detail on purpose — the underlying text can name a path, a hostname or the contents of a configuration — which leaves the operator with a true and unusable sentence. The id was already in the response and in the matching log line; only the rendering was missing. Finding this one took a person reading fifty journal lines and sending them on.

The simulator could never have caught this: it serves a configuration the same machinery generated, so by construction every document in it is one this build knows. The test fixture is now the simulator's own config with the operator's document appended — real secrets, real refusal — and it checks that the old path still fails before checking that the new one works, so a machinery that learns the kind will say so rather than quietly proving nothing.

The release you are running is marked as such again. A released build reports its version without a leading v — goreleaser stamps the tag with the v stripped — while this changelog spells versions exactly as the git tag does, so the two never matched and v1.16.0 marked nothing as "running here". The panel normalises instead of insisting, because neither side can simply adopt the other's spelling: the update script compares the tag with its v stripped against what the binary reports, so a binary carrying the v would look out of date on every run and reinstall itself forever.

Found by downloading v1.16.0 and running it, not by a test. Every test passed the version in the changelog's own spelling, and the browser check used a development build — which reports something like v1.16.0-4-gabc-dirty and matches no release at all, so the case that was broken looked exactly like the case that is supposed to match nothing.

The version this instance is running is now on screen, at the bottom of the sidebar, and clicking it opens this list. Until now the only way to find out which build a host was running was to ssh in and ask the binary, which meant nobody asked.
The first release of milestone v1.16 that is not a beta. Everything in the betas below is in it; nothing has been added but the version display.

One thing this release does NOT have, said plainly because the word stable does not say it: holzkube-manager has still never run on real amd64 hardware. Every operation below is proven against the Talos simulator and against a real Image Factory, and the single run that would close OPS-05 — a blank machine becoming a node through the wizard, taking a configuration, being upgraded — has not happened. Two constants remain estimates until it does: how long a machine may take to reappear after provisioning, and after an upgrade. Both are reported against elapsed time rather than enforced as timeouts, so a wrong number costs a misleading sentence and not a failed operation.

The update script would have tossed a coin over which archive to install. It took the first release asset whose name ended in linux_<arch>.tar.gz, and since holzkubectl got an archive of its own there are two of those. It now names the prefix that tells them apart, and more than one match is refused rather than resolved by luck.

A release is published rather than left as a draft, and a beta is deliberately not marked as a prerelease: the endpoint the update script reads skips both, so marking a beta as a prerelease would leave every host on the previous build while reporting itself up to date.

The release pipeline checks the release an operator would actually download — both Linux architectures present, exactly one daemon archive each, checksums there, and visible to the update script — because the build reporting success only means it uploaded what it built.

Removing a node from a cluster asks etcd first. Until now it did not read the membership at all: the refusal existed, on a different function, and the button went straight to leaving the cluster and then wiped the disk. The refusal was also wrong — it let the last voting member go. A majority of n is n/2+1, so four voting members tolerate exactly as many failures as three; four feels safer and is not.
Scaling a cluster is one view rather than two operations on nodes: what this cluster can spare, what adding or removing would mean, and why. It reaches etcd only when asked.
etcd can be restored from a snapshot, not only backed up. The README used to say so in the other direction: a backup that cannot be restored is a file, not a recovery.
kubeconfig without going through talosctl — the tool this product exists to replace.

Users, roles and service accounts. Machine labels, machine classes and cluster templates. A command-line client, holzkubectl, which is a client of this same API and not a second implementation of anything.

Disk encryption at install, with the node's own ID or its TPM. A static key is refused because for the STATE volume it ends up in plaintext in META, and a key server is refused because a node whose key server is gone does not boot — which reverses the decision this product stands on.

The installer image is resolved against the Image Factory instead of being assembled from parts. The old string was wrong three ways at once, each silently: it never carried SecureBoot, so a machine booted from a SecureBoot image installed a system that was not; it hardcoded one repository name; and it hardcoded the public Factory, so an installation pointed at a private one provisioned nodes that pulled from the public one.

The certificate countdown has a door: this installation's own client certificate can be renewed from the screen that warns about it. The new certificate is proved against a node before it replaces the one in use, so a failure changes nothing.
A node that answers but cannot be read is no longer indistinguishable from one that is absent. The two lead to different repairs — the cable or the power supply, against the node itself.

The first public release: the store and its forward-only migrations, the hash-chained audit log, authentication with a re-authentication window for destructive actions, the Talos transport seam with a deadline class per call, and the Image Factory screen.
